title: Replying to @danieldavid2.0 my two cents for two minutes! #theatre #b...
transcript: is it fair to charge full price tickets for a theater production that's only about an hour long? and is it fair to be mad about it? I have a lot to say about this, unsurprisingly but first I have to give the disclaimer that for multiple reasons I am not in a position to tell you what a theater ticket is worth to you ultimately this will all boil down to just “make your own ticket buying decisions however you want” but I do have some thoughts about the finances of short productions and also the metrics we're using to consider whether something is a satisfying evening at the theater. historically this conversation has frustrated me because theater is not a parking meter; you're not paying for time you're paying to be told a story. and ideally every show would be as long or as short as needed to be the best show it can be frankly I think a lot of 90 minute plays would be better if they were 20 to 30 minutes shorter, and personally in my busy schedule if a show is only an hour long that's a bonus! that's time I got back: I got to see a show AND go out with my friends or run errands or go to bed early or whatever but I also have an unusual relationship to theater. I'm squeezing in as much as possible while trying to keep my personal life afloat. but for a lot of people especially on Broadway and in the West End, theatre is a special night out and if you're thinking of it as something keeping you entertained for the evening then it makes a bit more sense to think of it in terms of cost per runtime. the problem is, *especially* on Broadway and in the West End, it's not practical to lower the ticket price based on runtime, because the running costs are probably about the same: the paychecks, the theater rental. and per the unions, there's a cap on the number of performances per week. so you can't even use that time to increase supply. By contrast, this comment was on my video about the shortest shows I've ever seen, which were produced much more nimbly often in unconventional found spaces they were supported by non-profit institutions so they were actually free to attend but then again charging a regular ticket price for a show that's under 30 minutes might have been hard for them to get away with anyway. despite what I said before about run time not equating to quality I can admit that there probably is a tipping point where the runtime gets so short that it becomes not impossible, but extremely difficult to really tell a story that leaves a satisfying impact. Having said that, in my personal opinion, a one hour runtime is not that tipping point. I think it's entirely possible and in fact extremely common for a one hour show to be a phenomenal, moving, memorable, satisfying evening at the theater
